name: Spermidine
lead: Spermidine is a naturally occurring polyamine (C7H19N3) found in all living cells, first isolated from semen, and present in foods such as wheat germ, soybeans, mushrooms and aged cheese [1][2][3]. It is a precursor to spermine and takes part in cell growth, membrane function and RNA and DNA stabilisation [1]. It is sold as an oral supplement, often as wheat germ extract, and is promoted as an autophagy-inducing longevity compound [4][5].

Its profile rests largely on laboratory and animal work. A 2009 Nature Cell Biology paper reported that spermidine extended lifespan in yeast, flies, worms and human immune cells through autophagy, and a 2016 Nature Medicine paper reported cardioprotection and lifespan extension in mice [6][7]. Observational data link higher dietary polyamine intake with lower cardiovascular and cancer-related mortality, but randomised human trials remain few and small, and no study has shown a cosmetic benefit in people [4][8][9].

Wikipedia also notes a laboratory finding that spermidine promoted hair shaft elongation in cultured hair follicles; this has not been established in clinical hair-growth trials [1]. In bodybuilding forums spermidine is discussed as a longevity hack, typically via wheat germ [2][10].

paras: Spermidine is an aliphatic polyamine. In plants and some bacteria it is formed from putrescine by spermidine synthase, and it is the precursor of spermine and thermospermine; some gut bacteria make it through a different two-enzyme route [1]. Cellular levels are tightly regulated, and reviews state that polyamine levels decline with age and are altered in some diseases, including Parkinson's disease [11][6]. Gut microbial production and dietary intake both contribute to the body's supply [12][13].

Spermidine was originally isolated from semen, which gave the compound its name [1]; a 1976 Annual Review of Biochemistry article reviewed the biochemistry of putrescine, spermidine and spermine [14]. Interest in longevity grew after a 2009 report that spermidine induces autophagy and promotes longevity in several organisms [6], followed by mouse cardioprotection data in 2016 [7] and a 2018 Science review framing spermidine as a caloric restriction mimetic [4]. A 2021 study reported that dietary spermidine improved cognitive function in fruit flies and related models [15].

Wikipedia reports that spermidine lengthened hair shafts and upregulated epithelial stem cell-associated keratins K15 and K19 in laboratory hair-follicle models [1]. No clinical trial of oral or topical spermidine for hair growth or skin appearance is reported in the sources reviewed here. A registered gel trial uses spermidine for peri-implant mucositis rather than cosmetic outcomes [16].
Spermidine has been studied for cognition, hypertension, vaccine response in older adults, coronary artery disease, lipids and obesity, and radiation-induced dry mouth [8][17][18][19][20][21][22].

Autophagy is the main proposed mechanism: spermidine is reported to inhibit the acetyltransferase EP300, raising acetylation of tubulin and promoting autophagy, and possibly to act through the MAPK pathway [1][5]. Spermidine also supports hypusination of eIF5A, linked to mitochondrial function and immune cell activity, and reviews describe effects on inflammation, lipid metabolism and the gut barrier [5][13][23][1]. Cardioprotection in mice involved enhanced cardiac autophagy and mitophagy [7].

A small registered study examined bioavailability of spermidine in healthy men, and an exploratory randomised trial in older men found that 40 mg per day had minimal effects on circulating polyamines [24][9].

A randomised clinical trial in older adults with subjective cognitive decline, published in JAMA Network Open in 2022, tested longer-term spermidine supplementation on memory performance and biomarkers [8]. A 2026 pilot randomised study in healthy older adults examined effects on immune cell senescence and vaccine responses [18], and a registered trial examined spermidine-induced autophagy and COVID-19 vaccination [19]. An exploratory trial in older men found minimal changes in circulating polyamines at 40 mg per day [9], and a pilot dose-escalation study tested a fasting-mimetic blend including spermidine in healthy young men [25].

Registered trials include studies on hypertension, blood lipids in overweight individuals, polyamine treatment in elderly coronary artery disease, metabolic responses in healthy adults, and healthy-ageing biomarkers [17][21][20][26][27]. A cohort study related plasma polyamines to short-term outcomes after ischaemic stroke [28]. Reviews note that most evidence comes from cell and animal studies, and that human randomised data are preliminary [4][5].

Human trials of oral spermidine have generally reported good tolerability at studied intakes, with mild gastrointestinal effects possible [8][9]. Polyamines are needed by rapidly dividing cells, and reviews discuss both anticancer immune effects and the theoretical possibility of supporting tumour growth in some contexts [4][13]. A review on polyamines in Parkinson's disease describes both neuroprotective and neurotoxic effects depending on context [11].

T Nation writers have promoted wheat germ as a food source and described spermidine as a longevity compound shown in animals to extend lifespan by as much as 25 percent, while noting the joke-prone name and that supplements exist [2][10]. A calorie-restriction article lists it alongside resveratrol as a longevity compound [3].

lore.intro: Spermidine is discussed in training forums as a longevity and autophagy supplement, usually via wheat germ extract [2][10].

claims.claim: Spermidine extends lifespan by inducing autophagy
claims.believers: T Nation articles state that animal models show lifespan extensions as large as 25 percent [2].
claims.experts: Lifespan extension is reported in yeast, flies, worms and mice, but evidence for lifespan effects in humans is lacking [6][7][5].

claims.claim: Eating wheat germ or other spermidine-rich foods is a practical way to get the benefit
claims.believers: T Nation writers recommend wheat germ as a spermidine source [2][3].
claims.experts: Observational studies link dietary polyamine intake with lower mortality, but they cannot establish causation and no trial has tested food-based dosing [4].

claims.claim: Spermidine improves memory and brain health
claims.believers: Supplement promotion cites animal cognition studies [15].
claims.experts: A randomised trial in older adults with subjective cognitive decline tested memory outcomes, and reviews describe human evidence as preliminary [8][4].

claims.believers: Wikipedia reports the lab observation that spermidine lengthened hair shafts in cultured follicles [1].
claims.experts: No clinical trial in humans has tested spermidine for hair growth.
